title: Transformer Turns Ratio

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Alternating Current

explanation: For an ideal (100% efficient, no losses) transformer, the ratio of secondary to primary voltage equals the ratio of secondary to primary number of turns, and — since power is conserved (VpIp = VsIs) — current has the INVERSE ratio: a step-up transformer (Ns > Np) increases voltage but proportionally decreases current, and a step-down transformer does the opposite.

variables.meaning: Number of turns in primary and secondary coil

workedExample.scenario: A step-up transformer with Np = 100, Ns = 1000, primary voltage 220 V.
workedExample.result: Vs = 2200 V (current correspondingly decreases by the same factor of 10)

commonMistakes: Assuming a step-up transformer increases both voltage AND current — an ideal transformer conserves power, so increasing voltage always comes with a proportional DECREASE in current, never an increase in both.

Applying the turns ratio formula to a transformer running on DC — transformers work only with ALTERNATING current, since they rely on a continuously CHANGING flux to induce EMF via mutual inductance; a steady DC current produces no changing flux and hence no induced EMF.
genZNote: Step-up transformer: more voltage, less current — power's just getting redistributed, not created.
